episodes.211646: A line of heavy thunderstorms moved east through northwest Alabama shortly after daybreak. The storms produced gusty winds knocked down a few trees. The rainfall contributed to a pickup truck hydroplaning off of westbound U.S. Highway 72 and into Shoal Creek near the Shoal Creek bridge, killing the occupant.
episodes.211696: Severe thunderstorm activity occurred across southern portions of Central Alabama from the evening of May 6 into the overnight hours of May 7. Most of the severe weather occurred in the form of wind damage and hail from three distinct supercells across parts of Montgomery, Macon, Greene, Hale, and Sumter counties. Large hail, up to baseball size, was observed just east of downtown Montgomery and later near Forkland in Greene County. As training thunderstorms resulted in 3 to 5 inches of rain falling, several instances of flash flooding occurred in parts of Montgomery, Elmore, Autauga, Marengo, and Sumter counties.
episodes.212867: An approaching northern stream trough in combination with sufficient moisture resulted in the development of isolated high based convection across Utah on May 5th. This activity resulted in strong outflow wind gusts, and at least one instance of an isolated severe wind gust.
episodes.213174: A line of strong thunderstorms with gusty winds rolled east through southern middle Tennessee shortly after daybreak, downing a few trees.
episodes.213445: A slow moving cold front sagged southeast across the area sparking a broken line of thunderstorms that moved across eastern OH and northwestern PA in the evening hours. A narrow axis of 100-250 J/kg of MLCAPE and 30 knots of effective shear supported a localized damaging wind threat resulting in power poles and trees down.
episodes.213446: A slow moving cold front sagged southeast across the area sparking a broken line of thunderstorms that moved across eastern OH and northwestern PA in the evening hours. A narrow axis of 100-250 J/kg of MLCAPE and 30 knots of effective shear supported a localized damaging wind threat resulting in power poles and trees down.
episodes.213557: A line of storms approached the Mississippi River, posing primarily a damaging wind threat. However, given the timing of the line crossing the area, the flash flooding risk heightened. Storms trained as a frontal boundary sunk south. A majority of the region experienced heavy rainfall the day prior during the morning hours, additional rains from this system continued to agitate rivers and streams. A storm trained right over the Memphis Metro resulting in flash flooding.
episodes.213660: A significant severe weather outbreak across northeast Louisiana and central and southern MS amid a favorably sheared environment. A capping inversion limited early convection, which allowed for higher instability. Supercell initiation began in the afternoon and eroded the capping inversion to allow a long track supercell to take root. This supercell produced a long track EF-3 tornados. Several other brief, weak tornadoes occurred. Supercells also produced hail as large as baseballs and straight line wind damage also occurred. The duration of rainfall also lead to flash flooding.
episodes.213817: A slowly advancing cold front was positioned beneath strong west-southwesterly flow downstream of a broad upper-level trough with embedded shortwaves. A moist low level layer and strong instability combined with strengthening deep-layer and low-level wind shear to support discrete supercells across southwest and southern Mississippi during the late afternoon and evening. These storms produced large hail and multiple tornadoes over southwest Mississippi, one EF1 and one EF2 tornado.
episodes.213953: Thunderstorms developed along a cold front that moved through South-Central Texas. Some of these storms produced large hail.
episodes.213964: The 2026 spring breakup along the Yukon River was highly dynamic, defined by a combination of thermal ice decay and severe mechanical ice jams. Because of an exceptionally cold winter and a cool spring, the river ice was thicker than normal and had not deteriorated significantly before the main breakup front arrived. Early-season flooding was driven by localized snowmelt and ice jams on independent river systems and upper sections of the Yukon River.
episodes.214028: The combination of multiple frontal boundaries draped across central Arkansas in cohesion with approaching H500 troughs led to an atmosphere that was conducive for the development of multiple storms across the state. The majority of these isolated storms would remain strong, but a few managed to become severe producing a few instances of severe wind gusts and large hail. Additionally, as cold air aloft remained increasingly cold and air at the surface became increasingly hot multiple cold air funnels were noted with a few strong thunderstorms across the state.
episodes.214063: A few severe thunderstorms produced large hail across the Northwest Hill Country.
episodes.214075: A cold front stalled across the region while multiple short waves moved overhead. This produce multiple days of unsettled weather.

A NWS ground survey confirmed an EF-1 tornado with maximum sustained winds of 90 mph tracked across portions of southeast Pike. This tornado began near Smithburg, MS at the intersection of Mount Herman Road Silver Drive where it uprooted a tree and snapped branches. Additional EF-0 tree damage was identified on Blanchard and Smithburg roads. The tornado peaked in intensity as an EF-1 as it crossed over Harold Alford Road uprooting and snapping several trees as well as taking down wooden transmission lines. At this point, the tornado exited Pike County and entered Walthall County.

A NWS ground survey confirmed an EF-1 tornado with maximum sustained winds of 90 mph tracked across portions of southeast Pike County and entered Walthall County near Harold Alford Road. It was  uprooting and snapping several trees as well as taking down wooden transmission lines as it traversed this area. The tornado then weakened caused EF-0 damage to trees as it crossed Brockdale Rd and the Bogue Chitto River. The end point of this tornado is estimated to be after it crossed MS Hwy 27 after it caused additional tree damage in a confluent pattern.

This summary covers primarily the Wilkinson County, MS portion of the track. For more information regarding this tornado please refer to WFO Jackson, MS's public information statements. The damage path of a large and significant tornado began between E Sibley Farms Rd and US Hwy 61 in Adams County, MS. Gray Sky/Vexcel and Sentinel-2 high-resolution satellite imagery was heavily leveraged over this rural and inaccessible portion of the track. The tornado produced occasional swaths of defined EF-1 tree damage as it moved into Wilkinson County along the Homochitto River and the damage path became apparently much larger and more multi-vortex in nature with several swaths of damage noted from vortices along and south of the mean path. The sheer amount of tree damage that extended over a half mile south of the mean track made it difficult to differentiate between RFD and subtornadic vortex damage, but the ingestion of this vorticity clearly assisted in rapid intensification of this tornado beyond Possum Corner, MS. An increasingly intense and large swath of downed trees began near Possum Corner Road, south of the Homochitto River. Widespread deforestation became increasingly evident as the tornado tracked east-northeast with several swaths of greater than 80% deforestation rated EF-2 for widespread snapped trunks of pine and mixed forest. The lack of well-built structures in the path of this tornado limited sampling of the peak rating of this tornado. As the tornado approached Doloroso-Rosetta Rd and the Homochitto River, the treefall pattern became cyclonic in orientation and indicative of a potential change of direction which is supported by Climavision V018 data from St. Francisville, LA. Near Old Hwy 61 Road and Perry Town Rd, barn and outbuilding structures were heavily damaged or destroyed. Almost all trees were snapped. High resolution satellite imagery also denoted numerous confluent swaths of damaging feeding into the main track from the south, indicative of subtornadic vortices and potentially a satellite tornado as it neared Old Hwy 61 Road. The tornado reached an initial peak width of 1200 yards here incorporating these feeder vortices. The tornado then continued east causing additional swaths of tree damage north of Perry Town Road before crossing the Homochitto River and back into Adams County. This tornado was continuously on the ground for approximately 81.9 miles over the span of 2 hours and 9 minutes through Adams, Wilkinson, Franklin, and Lincoln counties before concluding southwest of Monticello, MS in Lawrence County. This tornado peaked as an EF-3 east of Garden City, MS as well as near Thayer, MS in NWS Jackson's area of responsibility.
